query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the density and coherence of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries will increase creep resistance by acting as effective dislocation pinning sites, thereby reducing progressive plastic deformation under continuous high-stress, high-temperature loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating manufactured under standard deposition conditions, exhibiting a baseline interphase boundary density and coherence.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary deposition parameters—such as substrate temperature and cooling rate—to modify the FCC/BCC phase ratio and achieve an increased density and improved coherence of interphase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Testing under sustained high-temperature (e.g., around 1000–1400 K) and high-stress conditions (e.g., ~2–3 GPa) that simulate service environments where creep mechanisms dominate.
generation.structural_mediator: The FCC/BCC interphase boundaries that serve as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: An increased and more coherent network of FCC/BCC interfaces will constrain dislocation nucleation and motion by providing effective pinning, which in turn reduces the rate of creep deformation during continuous loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical testing conditions, samples with an enhanced FCC/BCC interface density are expected to show lower creep strain, reduced dislocation density and mobility, and delayed onset of plastic deformation compared to the baseline samples.
generation.baseline: Protective coatings produced with standard deposition parameters showing typical interphase boundary distribution and associated creep behavior.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under sustained high stress and high temperature regimes; its applicability outside these conditions (e.g., at lower temperatures or stresses) remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative effect of increased interphase boundary density on the creep rate is uncertain, and potential interactions with other mechanisms such as diffusion creep or grain-boundary sliding may also influence the results.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of coating samples by varying deposition parameters to systematically control FCC/BCC interphase boundary density and coherence while keeping alloy chemistry constant. Subject these samples to both nanoindentation and uniaxial creep tests under controlled high-temperature (e.g., 1200 K) and high-stress (e.g., 2.5 GPa) conditions.
measurements: Dislocation density and mobility via electron microscopy and diffraction techniques
Interphase boundary characterization (e.g., TEM/SEM imaging and quantitative phase analysis)
Stress-strain response analysis during creep testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples fabricated with increased FCC/BCC interphase boundary density and coherence do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain and dislocation mobility compared to baseline samples, then the mechanism of interface-mediated dislocation pinning as the dominant factor in creep resistance will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: The dynamic competition between the increase in FCC dislocation nucleation sites and the entanglement and annihilation of BCC dislocations leads to a reduction in the average number and length of dislocation lines in the system (Figure 3E).[  ] To accommodate deformation, dislocation lines suddenly cross phase boundaries into the FCC phase or undergo significant annihilation at 10% strain (Figure 3F), reducing the dislocation density in the BCC phase and significantly decreasing the number of dislocation lines in the system, providing ample slip space for subsequent strain (Figure 3G). This is called the phase boundary‐mediated mechanism. Therefore, this early strain localization mitigation mechanism and early strain‐hardening stability ability may benefit from the continuous dislocation nucleation and activation transfer under the mediated mechanism of BCC and FCC phase interfaces, thereby reducing dislocation accumulation.

In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys has predominantly focused on elucidating deformation mechanisms—ranging from slip system activation and stacking-fault network formation to phase transformation under load—and on quantifying creep behavior via simulation. For example, studies have examined diffusion‐controlled creep and grain-boundary sliding (e.g., in high-entropy superalloys) and protective coatings (with phase transformations driven by oxidation during HVOF deposition). However, while these investigations advanced our understanding of how intrinsic factors (alloy chemistry, grain structure, phase stability) influence mechanical response, they did not clearly isolate the role of the mixed FCC/BCC interphase boundaries. This interface, which might pin dislocations and thus impede progressive plastic deformation under continuous load, has remained an open question.
decision.unsolved: It still remains to be demonstrated whether and how the intrinsic microstructural feature of FCC/BCC interface density and coherence acts as a dominant factor in resisting creep deformation under sustained high-stress conditions, distinct from other mechanisms like diffusion or grain-boundary sliding.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the interphase boundary density and spacing by fine-tuning deposition parameters (e.g., substrate temperature and cooling rate) to control the FCC/BCC phase ratio and interfacial coherence.
decision.why: This approach logically follows the trend in previous studies that have assessed creep mechanisms in HE alloys but lacked controlled microstructural variations to pinpoint the role of FCC/BCC interfaces. By controlling the density and quality of these interfaces, the experiment can directly test whether an increased or optimized interphase network serves as a potent dislocation pinning mechanism, thereby enhancing creep resistance. Moreover, the design offers a clear basis for comparison against a baseline sample and provides measurable, falsifiable criteria in the form of altered creep rates and deformation patterns.
